overview: Borno became a renewed center of Sayfawa power west of Lake Chad after the court left Kanem. Scholarship, manuscript art and far-reaching diplomacy flourished across changing dynasties.

items.text: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Qurans combined Arabic commentaries with interlinear Old Kanembu translations. Spacious page layouts accommodated this layered reading.
Advanced students studied Arabic grammar, Old Kanembu and Quranic interpretation. Scholarly settlements linked learning with farming and royal privileges.
Between the fourteenth and eighteenth centuries, Borno maintained commercial and diplomatic ties reaching from Morocco toward Mecca.
Annotated manuscript production diminished during nineteenth-century political change, but oral translation and handwritten Qurans continued. The proposed causes remain scholarly interpretations.

sources.title: Rémi Dewière, The Kanem and Borno Sultanates (11th-19th Centuries) (2024)
Dmitry Bondarev, Shifting Regimes, Reshaping Manuscripts (2024)
